raw.answer: The case asked whether an Interior Ministry directive violated the Constitution. The directive said certain parts of a building, namely emergency stairs, driveways and arcades, cannot be registered as separately divided. The court held that the directive is consistent with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Interior Ministry's 1972 directive, which says emergency stairs, driveways and arcades are part of the building and cannot be divided for registration, fits the civil law rule and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Co-owners may ask at any time to divide jointly owned property, but the Civil Code article carves out an exception for things that cannot be divided because of the purpose they are used for.
The purpose of that exception is to increase the economic usefulness of jointly owned property and to avoid unnecessary disputes.
The shared parts of a building with separately owned units are indispensable to every unit owner's use of the building, so by nature they cannot be divided because of their use.
Land registration rules likewise say ownership of shared parts must pass together with the units and cannot be divided, which points to the same purpose.
The directive on emergency stairs, driveways and arcades matches this purpose, so it does not conflict with Articles 15 and 23 of the Constitution.
The petitioner's request for a unified interpretation did not meet the requirements of the Constitutional Interpretation Procedure Act, so it was not accepted.

who: Owners of units in divided buildings

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule on construction firms, and one of its official letters, could set punishments such as revoking a registration certificate or issuing a warning. The court decided they could not, because no law clearly authorized them. Both must stop being applied from the day the interpretation was announced.
raw.held: Article 31(1)(9) of the Construction Firm Management Rules (revoking a registration certificate after three or more violations within three years) and the Ministry's 1985 letter (a warning for a technician who could not perform duties for over a month) were not clearly authorized by law and conflict with the constitutional protection of people's rights. They must stop being applied from the announcement date.

points.text: Punishing people for breaking administrative duties limits their rights, so the conditions for punishment and its legal effects must be set by law. If a law delegates this to regulations, the delegation must be specific and clear.

A general delegation is read in light of the law as a whole, but regulations made under it may only cover detailed and technical matters of carrying out the law. They may not create sanctions beyond what the law authorizes.

Article 15(2) of the Building Act only generally authorizes the Ministry to make management rules for construction firms. It can be understood to cover registration requirements, conduct standards and supervision, but it does not clearly define its content or scope.

Revoking a registration certificate and issuing a warning with that effect are punishments that restrict rights, even though they serve the public interest and supervision. So the legal reservation principle applies to them.

The Building Act's Article 15 does not authorize revoking certificates, and Articles 85 to 95 already set out the conditions and sanctions for other violations. The rule and the letter therefore lack a clear legal basis.

who: Ministry of the Interior and other authorities that regulate construction firms

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in Taiwan's Business Tax Act is unconstitutional. The rule adds a late-filing fine or a neglect-to-file fine when a business does not file its sales figures or invoice detail statement on time. The court held the rule does not violate the Constitution, but said the authorities should review and revise how it applies when the business has already paid its tax.
raw.held: Article 49 of the Business Tax Act, which adds late-filing and neglect-to-file fines, is not in conflict with the Constitution. The competent authority should review and revise the rule where tax has already been paid, because the fine is a fixed percentage with no reasonable cap.

points.text: The rule aims to get businesses to file as the law requires, so authorities can reliably capture tax-source data and build a sound audit system.
The late-filing and neglect-to-file fines punish a failure to act (not filing), so they are administrative penalties for conduct, which is a separate matter from penalties for tax evasion.
The rule is necessary to advance the public interest, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
Where a business has already paid its tax, the fine is still a fixed percentage of the tax due with no reasonable maximum, so under Interpretation No. 327 the authority should review and revise it.
On the requirements for administrative penalties, the court noted that Interpretation No. 275 had already addressed them.

who: Businesses that file sales figures late
Businesses that have already paid their tax

raw.answer: The case asked whether a judge may ask the Constitutional Court to interpret the constitution when the judge believes a law they must apply conflicts with it. The court decided that judges may do so. They must still apply a law in force and may not simply refuse to apply it as unconstitutional.
raw.held: A judge who, on reasonable conviction, believes a law to be unconstitutional may suspend the case and ask the Justices for an interpretation, giving concrete objective reasons. The parts of Article 5, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Constitutional Court Procedure Act that do not match this must stop being applied.

points.text: The constitution is the highest norm, and deciding whether a law conflicts with it, and declaring it void, belongs exclusively to the Justices of the Judicial Yuan.
Judges judge independently according to law, so they must use a validly promulgated law as the basis for judgment and may not declare it unconstitutional and refuse to apply it.
Because the constitution outranks statutes, judges have a duty to obey it first, so a judge with a reasonable doubt about a law's constitutionality should be allowed to seek an interpretation first.
Courts at any level may suspend proceedings on this preliminary question and apply, giving concrete objective reasons for their conviction. They are not limited by the level of the court.
This removes the judge's difficulty in choosing between obeying the constitution and applying the law, and avoids wasting judicial resources.
Modern constitutional states set up judicial review of laws to protect the constitution's supremacy and judicial independence, and Taiwan's system is closer to the European model.

who: Judges of courts at all levels

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional that people who were given several short prison terms, each of which could be paid off with a fine, lose that option when the combined sentence goes over six months. The court found this puts an unnecessary limit on people's freedoms and does not fully fit Article 23 of the Constitution. It said the criminal law rules involved should be reviewed and revised.
raw.held: Where each separate sentence is six months or less and could be converted to a fine, but the combined sentence set under the joint-punishment rule exceeds six months so conversion is barred, this does not fully fit Article 23 and the rules should be revised. The part of Article 41 limiting fine conversion to sentences of six months or less, for these cases, stops being effective one year after the ruling is announced at the latest.

points.text: The joint-punishment rules for several crimes decided before a final judgment were not meant to leave the convicted person worse off.

Where each crime carries a heavy maximum of three years or less and each sentence is six months or less, a person facing hardship over body, education, job or family could normally pay a fine instead of serving time under Article 41.
When the combined sentence exceeds six months, the fine option is lost and the person must serve time, even though it was available for each sentence on its own.
This is an unnecessary restriction on people's freedoms and rights and does not fully match Article 23 of the Constitution.
The rules should be revised together with related issues, such as how to credit a part of the sentences already served.

who: People convicted of several crimes before a final judgment
People whose separate sentences are each six months or less
People whose combined sentence exceeds six months

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1990 announcement by the Department of Health (Executive Yuan) listing amphetamines as a chemically synthesized narcotic under the Narcotics Control Act was unconstitutional. The court decided it was not. It reasoned that the announcement only confirmed which items are managed and did not add penalties or new duties for people.
raw.held: The Department of Health's October 9, 1990 announcement placing amphetamines in the chemically synthesized narcotics category does not conflict with the Constitution, because it only confirms an item for control and adds no penalty or obligation.

points.text: The Narcotics Control Act expressly lists chemically synthesized narcotics and their preparations as one kind of narcotic, in Article 2, item 4.
The Act's enforcement rules define chemically synthesized narcotics as drugs made from chemical materials that are addictive or can be made addictive.

Long-term amphetamine use brings tolerance, psychological and physical dependence, delusions and hallucinations, abnormal behavior, and tendencies toward violence and antisocial acts, harming individuals and public peace.
Because amphetamines are addictive, they count as a narcotic under Article 2, item 4 of the Act.
The announcement only confirms the item as managed, which under Article 3 of the Act does not add penalties or duties for people, and it is needed to maintain social order and the public interest.

who: People who use or possess amphetamines
Medical providers (use in medical care is barred)

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Labor Insurance fee schedule violates the Constitution by limiting payment for jaw-correction surgery to injury or jaw-joint pain cases. The court decided that the limit does not go beyond what the Labor Insurance Act authorizes and does not conflict with the Constitution. Congenital chronic conditions or deformities that arose before a worker joined the insurance are outside coverage.
raw.held: The schedule's rule that jaw-correction surgery is limited to injury or jaw-joint pain cases, with no payment for pre-enrollment congenital conditions or deformities, stays within the Act's authorization and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Under Article 19(1), insurance benefits can only be claimed for insured events that occur after coverage begins and before it ends.
Labor insurance is social insurance, and Article 44 excludes cosmetic surgery from medical benefits to avoid wasting social medical resources, so cosmetic surgery is not covered.

Laws cannot cover every detail, so the legislature may authorize the authorities to issue supplementary rules on technical and detailed medical matters. Article 51 provides for payment under the fee schedule, which the central authorities set under its paragraph 2.
The schedule's jaw-correction rule (injury or jaw-joint pain, approved case by case) identifies cases that are both insured events within the coverage period and not cosmetic surgery.

Congenital chronic conditions or deformities that arose before the worker joined the insurance are not covered, so not paying for them does not exceed the Act's authorization or conflict with the Constitution.

who: Workers with congenital jaw conditions or deformities from before enrollment
Workers with jaw injury or jaw-joint pain

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government agency, after an administrative court cancels its earlier decision, may issue a new decision that simply repeats the old one. The court held that it depends on why the decision was cancelled. If the facts were unclear, the agency may investigate again and keep its view if the facts support it. If the court said the agency's legal reasoning was wrong, the agency is bound by the court's view.
raw.held: If an administrative court cancelled a decision because the facts were unclear, the agency may re-investigate and, if the findings support it, keep its earlier view. If it was cancelled because the agency's legal interpretation was wrong, the agency must follow the court's legal view. The part of the 1971 precedent (行政法院六十年判字第三十五號) that conflicts with this violates the constitutional right to sue and may not be applied.

points.text: The constitution's Article 16 gives people the right to ask a court to resolve disputes over their rights and duties through legal procedure and get a final resolution.
Article 4 of the Administrative Litigation Act says administrative court judgments bind the agencies concerned, which protects the right to a final resolution.
So an agency must respect a judgment cancelling its decision, and any new decision must follow the judgment's content so the person who sued actually gets relief.
Where the judgment said the facts were unclear, the agency may investigate again and, if the facts show its earlier application of the rules was not wrong, may keep its earlier view.
Where the judgment said the agency's legal interpretation was wrong, the agency is bound by the court's legal view and may not go against it.
The precedent says an agency may repeat its earlier view on re-examination; to the extent it conflicts with these points, it violates the right to sue and is not to be applied.

who: People who sue over administrative decisions
Government agencies whose decisions are cancelled

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries could refuse to hear any request to re-examine a decision that had itself been a re-examination. The court held that this blanket refusal went beyond what the law allows and violated the constitution, so those precedents may no longer be relied on.
raw.held: The statute's phrase "disciplinary case decisions" includes re-examination decisions. Commission precedent No. 335 and similar precedents that restrict public servants' litigation rights beyond the law conflict with the constitution's legal-reservation principle (Article 23) and are no longer to be applied from the date of the interpretation.

points.text: The Commission's published precedents are treated like court precedents, so they can be reviewed when the Commission relies on them in deciding cases.
The constitution protects the right to sue, but procedures for relief must be set by law. Public servants' right to seek relief may be limited only by law, not by a precedent.

A re-examination decision is made under the same statutory procedure as the first decision, so its nature does not differ because it comes later. Criminal, civil and administrative procedure also allow further review of re-trial judgments.

The statute's words "disciplinary case decisions" are not limited to the first decision. A re-examination decision may be challenged on a different ground, except that the same ground cannot be raised again.
Because of the 30-day deadline and the bar on repeating the same ground, an error in a re-examination decision might otherwise never be corrected. Refusing re-examination would be unfair.

The Commission's precedents that flatly bar re-examination of re-examination decisions conflict with this reading. They restrict public servants' rights beyond the law and violate Article 23, so they are no longer to be applied.

who: Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries

raw.answer: The case asked whether orders from Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs (in 1972 and 1986) were unconstitutional. The orders temporarily kept certain coal mining areas off-limits to public applications. The court decided the orders do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry's 1972 order and 1986 letter, which temporarily reserve coal mines (including mines whose rights were revoked or cancelled) and do not open them to applications, are guideline-type instructions to lower-level authorities and do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Minerals attached to land belong to the state, and under the Mining Act mining is not allowed without obtaining mining rights under that Act.

Article 34 of the Mining Act lets authorities refuse applications that harm the public interest or have no business value, and lets the Ministry stop accepting applications in a designated area, so authorities have discretion to approve or reject.
Taiwan's coal mines have poor natural conditions, high costs and worsening working conditions, so coal policy should put miners' safety and economic efficiency first.

The 1972 order reserved coal mines with revoked or cancelled rights so neighboring mines could expand, run more rationally and improve safety management; the 1986 letter repeated this and extended it to mineral types that include coal.
Both were guideline-type instructions from the central authority to lower authorities under those provisions, did not go against the law's purpose, and so do not conflict with the Constitution.

who: People applying to explore or mine coal

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter was unconstitutional. The letter said that when a suspended employee is later reinstated and paid all the back salary at once, the pay is taxed in the year it is actually paid, at the full amount paid. The court held the letter consistent with the income tax law and not in conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1971 letter is consistent with the income tax law and does not conflict with the Constitution. Income belongs to the year it is actually received, so lump-sum back pay is taxed by its payment date and total amount.

points.text: Choosing between taxing when cash is received and taxing when income is earned has pros and cons either way, and the choice is left to the legislature.

The income tax law, unlike its rule for business income, taxes individuals on the date income is actually received. The ruling reads this from articles 14 and 88, with the exception in article 76-1 for comparison.

Individual income tax therefore depends on whether income has been realized in the year. Cash or its substitute that has been received is taxed, while income not received for legal or practical reasons is not counted.
The letter taxes lump-sum back pay by its actual payment date and total amount, which matches this approach, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

The court noted that suspended public servants who received no pay or allowance differ from taxpayers who can shift when their income is paid. Whether taxing such long-accumulated income in full in one year is appropriate should be reviewed when the law is amended.

who: Taxpayers paid back salary in a lump sum
Public servants suspended and later reinstated
Tax authorities and the Ministry of Finance

raw.answer: The case asked whether an Interior Ministry directive saying a name cannot be treated as improper just because of how it sounds or what it suggests when spoken was unconstitutional. The court held that the directive does not fit the constitutional protection of personality rights. It said a name that sounds improper can be a special reason to apply for a name change.
raw.held: The Interior Ministry's 1976 directive saying that an improper name cannot be broadened to cover its sound or the meaning it suggests when spoken is inconsistent with the protection of personality rights and must no longer be applied.

points.text: The right to a name is a personality right; a name expresses a person's personality, so choosing a name is a freedom protected by Article 22 of the Constitution.

The Name Act lets people apply to change a name that is crude or improper in meaning, or for a special reason recognized by the authority. The authority decides whether a special reason exists in each case based on the specific facts.
Whether a name is elegant or improper depends on the name holder's own subjective values, and the authority should respect this when deciding.
A name's characters and its sound and suggested meaning are inseparable, so a name that sounds improper counts as a special reason to apply for a change.
The directive conflicts with this and with the protection of personality rights, so it should not be applied.

The court accepted the case because the Administrative Court's judgment, though it did not name the rule, rested on the directive, and a rule used as the basis of a judgment can be reviewed for constitutionality.

who: People who want to change a name that sounds improper
The Interior Ministry and other name-change authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1990 regulation on land-grant certificates for anti-communist soldiers treated officers unfairly compared with soldiers. Officers who had left their units in Taiwan without a post had military status but could not get certificates because they were not in the ranks. The court decided the provision was a fair way to handle this and did not conflict with Article 7 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 10 of the 1990 Regulations on Handling Soldier Land-Grant Certificates, which treats certain retired or discharged officers without posts as having already received certificates, was a fair measure. It did not create different treatment between officers and soldiers and does not conflict with Article 7 of the Constitution.

points.text: Officers without posts who had left their units in Taiwan were people who had been suspended, left unassigned, discharged, or left their posts without being retired. The defense ministry registered them in 1954 and kept their military status.
Even after the 1951 land-grant regulation, these officers still had military status.
That regulation gave certificates only to soldiers currently serving in the forces for two years or more, so officers not in the ranks could not get certificates.

Article 10 of the 1990 regulations addresses this situation by treating qualifying officers as already issued certificates, and it is a fair-minded rule rather than one that treats officers and soldiers differently because of rank, so it does not conflict with Article 7.

who: Retired or discharged officers without posts who left their units in Taiwan
Soldiers covered by the land-grant regulation

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule limiting who may receive a land registration agent certificate is unconstitutional. The court decided the rule does not go beyond what the law authorized and does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 4 of the Ministry of the Interior's 1990 land registration professional agent management rules, which lists who may request an agent certificate, stays within the authority the law gave and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Laws cannot spell out every detail, so they may authorize an agency to set detailed or technical matters by order. Such an order is constitutionally acceptable if it stays within the authorization and serves its purpose.

Article 37-1, paragraph 2 of the Land Law (requiring passing an exam or screening, with exceptions for existing practitioners) was made under Article 86, item 2 of the Constitution and does not conflict with it, as Interpretation No. 352 already stated.

The 1990 management rules were issued under the authorization in paragraph 4 of that Land Law article, and their Article 4 (certificate for those who passed the exam or screening, or who hold the registered agent proof or card) does not exceed that authorization.

who: Existing land scriveners holding registration proof or cards

raw.answer: The case asked whether a land registration office may cancel a farmland ownership transfer after the certificate proving the buyer can farm has been revoked. The court decided that it may. Once the certificate is revoked, the basis for the registration no longer exists, so the office can revoke its approval and erase the registration.
raw.held: If the local office revokes a buyer's farming-ability certificate because the buyer lacked that ability, the original registration office may revoke its earlier approval and directly cancel the ownership transfer registration.

points.text: The Constitution's land policy favors supporting owner-farmers and people who use the land themselves. The Land Law limit that private farmland buyers must be able to farm reflects this, and a transfer that breaks the limit is void.

Registration relies on the farming-ability certificate. Once the certificate is revoked, the stated ground for approval no longer exists, so the approval is flawed and the office may revoke it and erase the registration. The Executive Yuan letter fits the Land Law and does not use an administrative order to change people's rights.

Although the buyer gets ownership through a sale contract, the administrative approval of the registration depended on the certificate. Without it a requirement is missing. Cancelling the registration does not decide the sale is invalid, so private-law rights are not ruled on, and disputes over the contract can go to civil court.

The limit serves the public interest. A buyer who knowingly gave false information to obtain the certificate has no claim to protection of reliance. Even where the agency's own mistake caused a false certificate, cancellation is still proper for the public interest, and the transfer is void under the Land Law. How to compensate reliance losses is a separate question.
A good-faith third party who relied on the registration and acquired land rights is not deprived of them because the registration was cancelled.

who: Good-faith third parties who acquire land rights

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule on registering factories could let authorities order a factory to stop work or shut down for breaking the rule. The court decided that Article 19, paragraph 1 of that rule had no basis in a statute or in a statutory authorization, so it does not fit constitutional requirements. The provision will lose effect within one year of the ruling's announcement at the latest.
raw.held: Article 19, paragraph 1 of the Factory Establishment Registration Rules, which allows partial or total stoppage or closure orders, lacks a legal basis and is inconsistent with the constitutional principle. It loses effect from the announcement date, at the latest when one year has passed.

points.text: Ordering a factory to stop work or close for breaking administrative duties limits people's work and property rights, so the conditions for such orders must be set by law under Article 23 of the Constitution and Article 5, item 2 of the Central Regulations Standard Act.

If a law lets a regulation fill in details, the purpose, content and scope of that authorization must be specific and clear before the regulation can be issued, as earlier interpretations Nos. 313, 360 and 367 said.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs' factory registration rules touch on rights protected by the Constitution, so they need a statute or a statutory authorization as their basis.

Article 19, paragraph 1 allows stoppage or closure for violating the rules, which restricts work and property rights, yet it has no statutory text and no statutory authorization behind it, so it fails these requirements.

who: People wanting to set up factories

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Public Functionaries Disciplinary Act is unconstitutional because it gives no ordinary appeal from the disciplinary committee's decisions, and how disciplinary bodies and procedures should be set up. The court held that having no ordinary appeal is not by itself unconstitutional. It also said the disciplinary body should be organized like a court and give the accused fair, full procedural protection.
raw.held: Lacking an ordinary appeal does not make the disciplinary decisions violate the constitutional right to sue (Article 16). But the disciplinary body should take the form of a court and follow due process, such as direct hearing, oral argument, adversarial hearing, defense, and a final statement; the relevant authorities should review and revise its organization, name and procedures.

points.text: The right to sue is an institutional guarantee whose details are set by legislation, but its core, the ability to seek court relief for rights violations, cannot be taken away.
How many court levels are guaranteed can be decided by the legislature according to the nature of each type of case.

Disciplining officials for misconduct is expressly within judicial power under the Constitution, so the lack of an ordinary appeal from the disciplinary committee's final decision does not breach Article 16.
The disciplinary committee exercises judicial power, and its members are judges in the constitutional sense.
Because discipline affects the constitutional right to hold public office, and its members are judges, the body should be organized as a court, including its organization and name.

Disciplinary hearings should follow due process, giving the accused full protection such as direct hearing, oral argument, adversarial hearing, defense and a last statement, to uphold the right to sue.

who: The disciplinary committee and its members
Authorities responsible for revising the disciplinary system

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Taipei City rule limiting who may apply to invest in building retail markets was unconstitutional. The rule required applicants to hold the use rights to all private land within the market site. The court held that this added a restriction the urban planning law does not contain, so the rule should not be applied.
raw.held: The Taipei City requirement that applicants hold use rights to all private land in the market site adds a limit not found in Article 53 of the Urban Planning Law, goes against the constitution's protection of people's rights, and is not to be applied. During the period the Statute for Encouragement of Investment was in force, applications to build public facilities must meet its Article 3.

points.text: Local administrative bodies may issue orders to fill in details needed to carry out a law, but those orders must not conflict with the law.

Article 53 of the Urban Planning Law lets approved private investors rent public land or ask the government to buy private land for them, and does not require applicants to hold use rights to all the private land.
The Statute for Encouragement of Investment, Article 58-1, rests on the same purpose by letting investors buy land through the government when negotiations fail.

Taipei's rule added a restriction the law lacks and conflicts with the law's aim of having governments help private investment in public facilities and improve urban development, so it goes against the constitution's protection of people's rights.
While the investment statute was in force, applicants to build markets had to meet its Article 3, which limits eligible businesses to joint-stock companies engaged in production.

who: Private persons or groups wanting to invest in building retail markets
Owners of private land within market sites

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Cabinet (the Executive Yuan) must resign as a whole after a new Legislative Yuan is elected. The court decided that the Premier must offer to resign to the President before the newly elected legislature first meets, and the Vice Premier, ministers and ministers without portfolio must resign along with the Premier.
raw.held: After a Legislative Yuan term ends and new members are elected, the Premier must submit his resignation to the President before the first session. The Vice Premier, heads of ministries and commissions, and ministers without portfolio must resign together with him.

points.text: The Constitution requires the Premier to be nominated by the President and approved by the Legislative Yuan, and the Executive Yuan answers to the Legislative Yuan.

Democracy rests on the will of the people and on accountability, so a government needs a popular basis to be legitimate; after a legislative election the top executive body should reorganize to reflect the latest public opinion.

Because the Premier needs the legislature's approval, he should resign before the new legislature's first session, so the President can review the political situation and nominate someone again for the legislature's consent.

The Vice Premier, ministry heads and ministers without portfolio are appointed on the Premier's proposal and attend Cabinet meetings and take part in policy decisions, so they should resign with him to show accountability.

Heads of Executive Yuan agencies who are not ministers without portfolio resign under ordinary administrative procedures, and those with legally fixed terms are not affected by the Cabinet's resignation.

who: The Premier (head of the Executive Yuan)
Vice Premier, ministry heads and ministers without portfolio

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Farmers' Association Act is unconstitutional for making a member leave the association when their registered address moves out of the association's area. The court held that it is not unconstitutional. It added that a member who moves but still farms should keep their status as an insured person under farmers' health insurance.
raw.held: The Act's rule that moving address out of the association's area ends membership does not conflict with Articles 7 and 10 of the Constitution. However, a member who moves but still farms must not lose their farmers' health insurance status, and may keep paying premiums and receiving coverage; the authorities' orders must follow this.

points.text: Farmers' associations serve farmers within their own area, so membership requires both living in the area and actually farming.
Ending membership when a member's address leaves the area is simply the natural legal consequence of that requirement.
Changing household registration is voluntary, so the rule does not violate the freedom of residence and movement in Article 10.
A person who still farms can apply to join the local association in their new area, so there is no violation of equality under Article 7.
Farmers' health insurance is social insurance and a right farmers hold by status, not dependent on being a member or being registered at the original insuring unit's location.
The insurance rules on insuring units only set the scope of the local associations' responsibility, so a farmer who moves but keeps farming stays insured and the authorities' orders must follow this.

who: Farmers' association members who move out of the area
Farmers who still farm after moving
Local farmers' associations and the authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's House Tax Act was unconstitutional in how it sets the basis for collecting the tax, the tax rates and the tax-exempt amount. The court held that the Act's provisions do not conflict with the Constitution. It also said the Act and the Land Act differ on owner-occupied homes, which can cause confusion, so the authorities should review and fix this.
raw.held: Articles 1, 5, 6 and 15 of the House Tax Act do not conflict with the Constitution, and neither does the single exemption amount for homes under Article 15, paragraph 1, item 9. The relevant authorities should review the house tax policy and amend the inconsistency between the Land Act and the House Tax Act on owner-occupied homes.

points.text: The Constitution's duty to pay taxes according to law means people owe tax on conditions set by law or may get tax relief under it, and the content of the law within reasonable limits is for the legislature to decide.

The House Tax Act already sets out the taxpayer, tax items, rates, payment method and period, so its provisions on the basis for collection, rates, local rate procedure and exemptions do not conflict with the Constitution.
Not distinguishing owner-occupied homes from other residential homes in the exemption means rented homes below a set value also get the exemption, but this is within the legislature's discretion.

House tax is a property tax. The old law split homes into owner-used and rented and taxed them differently, while the current Act taxes all by current value at one rate, and this does not violate equality or property rights.

The Land Act and House Tax Act are in a general-and-special law relationship, so the House Tax Act's rates apply first. But the Land Act exempts owner-occupied homes while the House Tax Act has no such exemption, which invites misunderstanding.
Such inconsistent provisions in the two laws should be reviewed and amended so that the laws are coordinated.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Ministry of Finance letters on how to calculate fines for using farmland for non-farm purposes were unconstitutional. The letters said the fine is based on the original land value increment tax exemption for the whole parcel, not just the part whose use was changed. The court decided the letters do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The three Ministry of Finance letters, which set how the fine under Article 55-2 of the Land Tax Act is calculated, fit that article's purpose, are necessary to stop illegal use of farmland and promote the public interest, and do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The state offers a land value increment tax exemption when farmland is transferred to farmers who farm it themselves, to keep and expand farm operating scale.
If the land is later transferred to a non-farming person or changed to non-farm use without legal authority, the Land Tax Act Article 55-2 provides a fine of twice the exempted tax amount.
The Agricultural Development Act sets a principle that each parcel of farmland may not be divided, so changing part of a parcel to non-farm use without legal basis is also not allowed.
The letters say the fine is based on the exempted tax for the whole land, not in proportion to the area wrongly used. This was an interpretation within the agency's authority that fits Article 55-2.
This method is necessary to deter illegal use of farmland and advance the public interest, so it is not unconstitutional.
The court added that the competent authority should still review whether fines of different amounts should apply depending on how serious the violation is.

who: Owners of farmland changed to non-farm use
Farmers who receive farmland under the tax exemption
Ministry of Finance and tax authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether several provisions of the Act for Investigating and Punishing Hoodlums (檢肅流氓條例), including police forced appearance and secret witnesses, violate the Constitution. The court ruled that Articles 5, 6, 7, 12 and 21 of the Act conflict with the Constitution's protections of personal liberty and the right to bring administrative appeals and lawsuits. They lose effect no later than December 31, 1996.
raw.held: Articles 6, 7, 12 and 21 of the Act are inconsistent with Article 8, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, and Article 5 conflicts with Article 16. All five lose effect from the date of the interpretation, and no later than December 31, 1996.

points.text: Any measure restricting personal freedom, whether or not the person is a criminal defendant, must follow a procedure set by law whose content is substantively fair and meets the conditions of Article 23.

Article 5 bars administrative appeals and lawsuits against a police decision labeling someone a hoodlum and issuing a warning, even though that decision harms reputation and may lead to loss of liberty. This violates Article 16.

Articles 6 and 7 let police force people to appear without any document from a judicial authority, treating them like caught-in-the-act offenders. This goes beyond what is necessary and ignores the Constitution's distinction between those caught in the act and others.

Article 12 on secret witnesses removes the right of the person and his lawyer to confront or cross-examine the witness. It also hinders the court in finding the truth and risks punishment on insufficient evidence.

Article 21 exposes people who have already been sentenced and served their punishment to further reformatory treatment, whether or not it is needed to prevent future offences. This risks irreversible loss of liberty, so it goes beyond what is necessary and lacks substantive fairness.
The court said the authorities should review the whole Act, balancing individual rights and public order.

who: Witnesses and accused persons in hoodlum cases

raw.answer: The case asked whether a business tax rule and a Ministry of Finance guideline could shift the duty to file and pay business tax from the business to the buyer at an auction. The court decided they could not, because the Business Tax Act itself set who must file and pay. It found the rules unconstitutional, and they lose effect within one year.
raw.held: The enforcement rules (Article 47) and the Ministry of Finance guideline (item 2) that make the auction buyer file and pay business tax conflict with the Business Tax Act and violate Constitution Articles 19 and 23. They lose effect no later than one year from the ruling's announcement.

points.text: Under Article 19 of the Constitution, taxpayers, tax items, rates, methods and tax relief must be set by law, and orders cannot provide differently.

Restrictions on people's rights must be set by law and not go beyond what is necessary (Article 23). Detailed rules may be delegated, but enforcement rules may cover only details and technical matters, and cannot contradict the parent law or add restrictions the law does not contain.
The Business Tax Act names businesses selling goods or services, and the receivers or holders of imported goods, as the taxpayers who must file and pay.
The enforcement rule and the guideline shifted the filing and payment duty to the auction buyer, which does not match the Act.
Even though business tax is added on top of the price and the buyer bears it, so no extra tax burden arose, the rules still imposed a filing and payment duty on buyers and so conflicted with the Act.
If the authorities think court or agency auctions of real estate need a different payer for operational convenience, that must be set by law.

who: Business owners whose goods are auctioned
Courts, customs and other auctioning agencies

raw.answer: The case asked whether legislators reviewing the budget may move money between budget items or add and cut items. The court decided that legislators may make reasonable cuts, but may not rewrite the budget line by line like a bill, nor shift amounts among items and add or cut original items.
raw.held: The Legislative Yuan has the power to review budgets and may make reasonable cuts. It may not move or increase amounts among the categories and items of an agency's budget, or add to or cut the original budget items, because this is forbidden by the Constitution.

points.text: The Legislative Yuan has the power to review budget bills under Article 63, and the way it reviews different kinds of bills differs because the bills differ in nature.
A budget bill differs from a law: only the Executive Yuan may propose it, it has time limits, and it records specific figures for one year, while a law sets abstract rules that apply repeatedly.

A budget is in substance an administrative act that takes legal form after legislative approval, so reviewing it is like approving the annual policy plan and it cannot be edited clause by clause like a law.
Moving money among items changes the content of the policy plan, leaves no one clearly responsible for success or failure, and so offends the separation of legislative and executive powers.
Article 70 bars the Legislative Yuan from proposing increased spending. An item that gains money through a shift is in substance such a proposal, even if the total stays the same.

Legislators still have other tools: they may decide to ask the Executive Yuan to change policies they disagree with, or make reasonable cuts to improper spending, which lets them oversee government and avoid wasteful spending.

who: The Executive Yuan and its agencies

raw.answer: The case asked whether a sitting President who runs for re-election still has immunity from criminal prosecution. The court decided that the President still has this protection under Article 52 of the Constitution, because being a candidate does not change the President's status as President. The campaign itself is still governed by the election and recall law.
raw.held: A sitting President running for re-election is still covered by Article 52 of the Constitution. Except for insurrection or treason, the President cannot be criminally prosecuted unless removed by recall or leaves office.

points.text: Article 52 protects the President from criminal prosecution, except for insurrection or treason, until recalled or out of office. It honors and protects the President's special status as head of state, who leads the armed forces at home and represents the Republic of China abroad.
The protection exists to secure the exercise of presidential powers, keep the political situation stable, and support normal foreign relations.

The immunity belongs to the office, not to the person, and it has limits. Insurrection or treason can still be prosecuted, and for other crimes prosecution is only temporarily blocked, so criminal law still applies.
A sitting President who runs for re-election is listed as a candidate, so the campaign is governed by the election and recall law. But the President's status as President does not change by running.

Because the Constitution ranks above statutes, a sitting President lawfully running for re-election cannot be prosecuted under the criminal law or the election and recall law, except for insurrection or treason, unless recalled or out of office.

raw.answer: The case asked whether prosecutors could be given the power to detain (remand) suspects, and whether the Habeas Corpus-style review law could require that an arrest be unlawful before a court review can be requested. The court decided that under Article 8 of the Constitution only a court made up of judges may decide on detention, so the Criminal Procedure Code provisions giving prosecutors that power conflict with it. It also found the review law's 'unlawful arrest' requirement unconstitutional.
raw.held: The Criminal Procedure Code provisions giving prosecutors detention powers, and the review law's requirement of 'unlawful' arrest, conflict with Article 8 and lose effect no later than two years after the interpretation is announced; the earlier Interpretation Yuan-Jie No. 4034 is changed. The 24-hour limit counts only time when investigation can actually be carried out, and legal obstacles consistent with the Constitution are not counted.

points.text: Investigation, prosecution, trial and punishment are all parts of criminal justice, so prosecutors are part of the broad 'judicial organs' in Article 8(1), though not the courts in the narrow sense.
Prosecutors are not part of the court: they must obey superiors, are not independent in the way judges are, and sit outside the court.
'Interrogation' (審問) and 'court' in Article 8 mean a court of judges with trial power, so only such a court may decide on detention. Other organs must send a suspect to court within 24 hours.

Detention is the heaviest interference with personal liberty and should be a last resort, so an independent trial body should decide whether it is lawful and necessary. The prosecutor-power provisions therefore do not fit Article 8(2).

Article 8(2) lets a suspect or others request court review without requiring that the arrest be unlawful, since lawfulness can only be judged after the court examines it. The review law's 'unlawful' condition conflicts with this, so the earlier interpretation built on it is changed.

The 24 hours counts only time when investigation can actually proceed. Court review time and constitutionally valid legal obstacles are not counted. The court rejected the arguments based on history, international conventions and prosecutors' role resembling investigating judges.

raw.answer: The case asked whether an old Supreme Court precedent, which says that excessive conduct by one spouse who is provoked by the other's misconduct is not automatically 'intolerable cohabitation abuse', is unconstitutional. The court held that it is not unconstitutional, because it does not stop the abuse rule in the Civil Code from applying once conduct goes beyond what a marriage can bear. The court also explained how 'intolerable abuse' is to be judged in each case.
raw.held: The precedent is not in conflict with the Constitution, because it does not exclude the Civil Code abuse provision from applying to excessive conduct that goes beyond what is tolerable for maintaining the marriage.

points.text: Protecting human dignity and personal safety is a basic constitutional idea, and it applies to marriage and family life too.
Spouses should respect each other and prevent domestic violence, which is needed to sustain marriage and expected by society.
The divorce provision on intolerable abuse exists to protect each spouse's dignity and personal safety, and divorce is allowed when continuing life together can no longer be expected.

Whether abuse is intolerable is judged case by case: how serious the harm is, the parties' education, social position and other circumstances, and whether the marriage is endangered. Abuse beyond what spouses can usually bear that harms dignity and safety counts.
The precedent only says that excessive conduct by a provoked spouse is not automatically intolerable abuse; if it has not endangered the marriage, it cannot ground divorce.

The precedent does not give a spouse a right to punish the other's misconduct, and it does not remove the Civil Code provision where conduct exceeds what can be tolerated, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the central government's construction bond law is unconstitutional. The rule said lost, stolen or destroyed bearer bonds could not be reported lost and payment stopped, and it excluded certain Civil Code protections. The court found the rule inconsistent with the Constitution's protection of property and of the right to seek legal remedies.
raw.held: Article 8, first part, of the construction bond issuance regulations conflicts with Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution. From the day of the ruling, it stops applying to bearer bonds issued under that regulation afterward.

points.text: The state's duty to pay holders of bearer construction bonds is essentially the same as any issuer's duty to pay holders of bearer securities.
The Civil Code provisions long protect bearer-security holders when securities are lost, stolen or destroyed, without harming good-faith third parties or adding to the issuer's burden.
The rule barred reporting a loss and stopping payment and excluded those Civil Code protections; its aim was to make the bonds easier to circulate for fiscal purposes.
Under the rule the treasury could be released from liability by paying even when it knew the holder had no right to dispose of the bond or had been notified of its loss, theft or destruction.
The rule also limited rightful holders from asking a court to declare lost, stolen or destroyed bearer securities invalid through the public summons procedure.

Lawful holders were left with no way to seek protection under the Civil Code rules and no other reasonable remedy, which conflicts with the property protection in Article 15 and the right to seek remedy in Article 16.

who: Lawful holders of bearer construction bonds
Holders whose bonds are lost, stolen or destroyed
The national treasury as bond issuer

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Land Act rule requiring land registration agents to pass an exam or screening, with a transition rule for people already working, is unconstitutional. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the Constitution. It found the transition period fair to people already working in the field.
raw.held: Land registration agents are a specialized profession whose qualifications must be set by law under Article 86, item 2 of the Constitution. Article 37-1, paragraph 2 of the Land Act (as amended on 29 December 1989) is consistent with this and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Land registration affects people's property rights, and agents need specialized knowledge and experience, so the work is a specialized profession.
Article 86, item 2 of the Constitution says qualifications for specialized professions must be determined by law through examination and screening.
The Land Act provision aims to build a sound system of land registration agents, which fits the constitutional rule.
Those already working who held a government-issued certificate or registration card are allowed to continue practicing.

Those working without a certificate or card had no lawful right to begin with, and the five-year period let them choose to take the exam or screening, or change careers, which balances their interests.
Because of that period, the rule raises no problem of applying the law retroactively.

who: Existing agents with certificates or cards
Unlicensed people already doing the work
People who use land registration services

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter ruling was unconstitutional. The ruling said foreign companies approved for incentives under the Investment Incentive Statute could keep their tax breaks after the statute's term ended, and that they also had to withhold 20% income tax when sending after-tax profits to their head offices. The court held that the ruling is consistent with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 24 September 1991 letter ruling does not conflict with the Constitution. A foreign company that keeps using the Investment Incentive Statute's tax breaks after it expires must also withhold 20% income tax on after-tax profits paid to its head office, under Article 16, paragraph 3.

points.text: The Constitution's duty to pay taxes according to law covers the taxpayer, tax item, rate, method and period. But when a tax law has related rights and duties, they must be applied as a whole and not arbitrarily split, for the sake of consistent application and balance.

The statute's purpose is that a foreign branch enjoying tax relief must also bear the withholding duty when it pays after-tax profits to the head office. Otherwise foreign companies could avoid Taiwan tax by setting up branches, so the two provisions are linked and cannot be applied separately.
The statute expired on 31 December 1990, but cases approved while it was in force (five or four years of exemption) continue to be governed by it, to protect investors' interests.

Since approved foreign companies still enjoy the tax exemption after expiry, the related head-office tax burden must also be withheld under Article 16, paragraph 3, in line with the original legislative intent.
The Ministry's letter ruling applies the statute as a whole and does not split it up arbitrarily, so it fits this reasoning and does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Foreign companies approved for incentives under the statute

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Ministry of Finance's rules on how businesses with both taxable and tax-exempt sales calculate their business tax, and its letter-ruling on dividends, were unconstitutional. The court decided that both are consistent with the Constitution. It added that the ministry should still review how the non-deductible ratio is calculated.
raw.held: The 1986 calculation rules rest on a clear authorization in the Business Tax Act and do not conflict with the principle that taxes must be set by law. The 1988 letter-ruling on dividends does not treat dividends as taxable and does not violate the Constitution, but the authority should review and improve the ratio calculation.

points.text: The Business Tax Act expressly authorized the Ministry of Finance to set the ratio and method for input tax that cannot be offset, because such tax is hard to divide clearly for businesses with mixed sales. A specific, clearly bounded tax authorization like this is not forbidden by the Constitution.
The calculation rules use a ratio method meant to make tax work easier for both sides, so they did not go beyond the authorization.

The 1992 amendment letting businesses with complete books choose a direct method was a reasonable improvement and does not make the original ratio method unlawful, since authorities may revise their rules within the law's purpose.
Dividend income is outside business tax's scope, and the letter-ruling only explains how dividends figure in calculating non-deductible input tax. It does not add output tax or tax dividends.
Leaving dividends out of the ratio would let related input tax be fully deducted, which is unfair compared with pure investment businesses and would encourage tax avoidance.

The letter-ruling's wording using dividends as the ratio base could be misread as extending business tax to dividends, and there are several ways to compute the ratio, so the authority should review and improve it.

who: Businesses with both taxable and tax-exempt sales
Businesses that also carry on investment activity

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court resolution was unconstitutional. It said that once neighbors had both pointed out a shared land boundary during a re-survey without dispute and the result was announced, a landowner could not later claim the boundary was wrong and sue to have it set again. The court held that this resolution conflicts with the constitutional protection of property and the right to sue, so it must not be applied.
raw.held: The Supreme Court's 1986 resolution (1), which treated a suit to reset a boundary as plainly without merit if the owner had earlier pointed out the boundary, conflicts with the constitutional protection of property rights and the right to sue. It must not be applied.

points.text: A Supreme Court resolution that a judge relies on in a ruling is treated like a regulation (an order), so people may ask the court to review whether it is constitutional.
The Constitution protects property rights and the right to sue. A court hearing a property dispute must decide it on the evidence, using experience and logic.
A re-survey of land maps is a technical service by the land authorities that records existing ownership accurately. It does not add to or reduce anyone's private rights.
After the announcement period ends, the survey result is final and the land authority must register the change, even if an owner objected that the boundary was pointed out wrongly.

An owner who still disputes the boundary may bring a civil suit. The court must decide it on the evidence and may not rule against the owner as plainly unfounded just because the boundary was earlier pointed out wrongly.
The resolution barred owners who had pointed out the boundary from claiming it was wrong. This conflicts with these principles, so it conflicts with the Constitution and is not to be applied.

raw.answer: The case asked what freedom of expression under Article 11 of the Constitution means for broadcasting and television. The court decided that speaking through radio and TV is protected free speech. The state must share out broadcast frequencies fairly and reasonably, and must respect ordinary people's equal right of access to the media while still protecting the media's editorial freedom, all through laws.
raw.held: Expression by radio and television falls within the free speech protected by Article 11. The state must allocate frequencies fairly and reasonably and respect equal public access to media, balanced against media editorial freedom, and must set all this out in law.

points.text: Free speech underpins democracy, and broadcasting is an important way for people to express views, so it is protected by Article 11.

Broadcasting reaches far and has deep social impact, so those who broadcast must act responsibly, and the state may lawfully restrict misuse such as harming public morals, social peace, national interest or others' rights.

Broadcast frequencies are a limited public resource, so the state should pass laws so that the authority allocates them fairly and reasonably, avoiding monopoly and giving people more chances to use media.

The right of access to the media lets the public ask media for space or time to express views, which helps keep reporting accurate and fair, for example through correction or reply, or candidate policy debates.

Access limits the media's choice and editing of content, and forcing media to carry all opposing views would take away editorial freedom and could weaken accurate, fair reporting, so access must be balanced with editorial freedom.
The conditions for access should be clearly set out in law, aiming at equality.

who: Members of the public seeking to use the media

raw.answer: The case asked whether the rules for taxing individuals' profit from selling a house were unconstitutional, in particular the method of setting taxable income when a seller cannot prove the price and cost. The court decided that the Enforcement Rules provision and the Ministry of Finance's 20% standard for Taipei in 1987 do not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 17-2 of the Income Tax Act Enforcement Rules, as amended in 1988, does not violate the principle that taxes must be set by law. The Ministry of Finance's 1988 notice setting Taipei's 1987 house-sale income at 20% of the house tax assessed value was set with year, area and economic conditions in mind, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Profit from an individual's house sale is a kind of property transaction income under Article 9 of the Income Tax Act.

When a taxpayer does not file or show documents, tax authorities may estimate income, which is not unconstitutional, but the estimate should be objective and reasonable, close to actual income, to keep taxes fair.
Applying one fixed percentage of assessed value regardless of year, area or economic conditions would stray from actual income and be unfair, as Interpretation No. 218 already said.

Article 17-2 lets sellers with proof of price and costs be taxed on actual figures, and otherwise the authorities apply a standard that local tax offices draft from the year's economic conditions and the housing market and the Ministry of Finance approves. This does not violate the principle that taxes must be set by law.

The 20% standard was based on a sample survey of many Taipei cases for 1987, where the average was 22.02% and 73% of cases were at 20% or above, and it was set with year, area and economic conditions in mind rather than as a fixed percentage, consistent with Interpretation No. 218.

who: Sellers who cannot prove price or cost

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent limiting retrial claims based on 'newly discovered evidence' violates the Constitution. The precedent says only evidence that already existed before the final fact-finding hearing ended, but that the party did not know about, counts. The court held the precedent does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Supreme Court precedent (1940 Shang-zi No. 1005) is not unconstitutional. Evidence that only came into existence after the final fact-finding hearing ended cannot be a ground for retrial, though whether the facts it shows are bound by the final judgment depends on each case.

points.text: Parties may submit attack or defense methods, including evidence, at any time before the fact-finding hearing ends, and the appeal court on law must rely on the facts the second instance settled. So parties should submit all existing, known evidence by then.
The binding effect of a final judgment is measured at the close of the fact-finding hearing, for the same reasons.
Holding back known, available evidence to use in a retrial later would abuse the retrial system, waste litigation efficiency and undermine the stability of final judgments.

The precedent pushes parties to submit all existing, known evidence early and prevents arbitrary retrial suits after a judgment becomes binding, protecting the stability of final rulings, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

Evidence that arose after the hearing ended cannot ground a retrial, but whether the facts it proves are bound by the final judgment depends on the individual case. Whether evidence made from earlier-existing evidence counts as newly discovered is a question of fact-finding and legal interpretation.

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules implementing the University Act were unconstitutional. The rules let the Ministry of Education set common required subjects for all universities and said students who fail them cannot graduate. The court held that two of these provisions went beyond the University Act and conflicted with the constitutional protection of academic freedom and university self-governance.
raw.held: Article 22, paragraph 1 (latter part) and paragraph 3 of the University Act's implementing rules are inconsistent with the Constitution. They lose effect no later than one year after the interpretation is announced.

points.text: Constitution Article 11 protects academic freedom as an institutional guarantee, which includes research, teaching and learning freedom and recognizes university self-governance.

Government supervision of universities must rest on law and meet the legal reservation principle of Article 23; the education authority should avoid intruding on matters protected by academic freedom.
Course design and subject setting relate to teaching and learning freedom, so how a university sets its curriculum falls within university autonomy.
The University Act does not authorize the Ministry to convene universities to set common required subjects, so the implementing rules cannot add restrictions the Act does not contain.

Making failure of common required subjects a bar to graduation limits graduation conditions, which belong to university autonomy under the cited University Act and degree law provisions, so that clause exceeds the Act.
During the one-year period, common required subjects should be set either by explicit statute or by each university through its own curriculum process.

raw.answer: The case asked whether an administrative court precedent was unconstitutional because it limits retrials based on forged or altered evidence. The Constitutional Court said the precedent is consistent with the constitutional protection of the right to sue. A retrial on this ground requires that the evidence was actually forged or altered, not merely claimed to be.
raw.held: The Administrative Court's 1987 precedent (76 Pan-Tzu No. 1451) does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution. Under it, forgery or alteration must be established by a final guilty judgment, or by a criminal case that cannot start or continue for reasons other than insufficient evidence.

points.text: Article 16 protects the right to sue, but the legislature decides the procedures and requirements for lawsuits by law, in a proper and reasonable way, according to the nature of the case.
A retrial for forged or altered evidence requires that the evidence was truly forged or altered, not just that the party who wants a retrial says so.
Forgery or alteration counts as proven only if a guilty judgment is final, or the criminal case cannot start or continue for reasons other than insufficient evidence.

A retrial is an extraordinary remedy against a final judgment and affects the stability of the legal order, so limits on bringing it are appropriate. The limits keep retrials from being unrestricted and protect the finality of judgments.
These requirements reflect the legislature's balance between legal stability and the correctness of judgments, so they are not unconstitutional.

The administrative litigation law's retrial grounds were drawn from the civil procedure provision, and the amendment did not intend to remove the requirement of a final guilty judgment. The precedent is therefore consistent with that law and does not conflict with Article 16.

who: People seeking a retrial in administrative cases
Parties to final administrative court judgments

raw.answer: The case asked how many National Assembly members must be present to open the first reading of a constitutional amendment. The court decided that the Constitution and the law do not set this number, so the Assembly may decide it for itself under its own self-regulation. Whether it uses one-third, two-thirds, or a number from general meeting rules, none of these conflicts with the Constitution.
raw.held: The two-thirds attendance and three-fourths vote in Article 174, item 1 apply only when the Assembly passes an amendment. The quorum for the first reading is left to the Assembly's own self-regulation, and any of the options is constitutional, provided the decision fits the free and democratic constitutional order.

points.text: Representative bodies may set their own procedures within the limits of the Constitution and law, which is called parliamentary self-regulation. The court had already explained this in Interpretation No. 342, and the amendment article on Assembly procedure follows the same idea.
Article 174, item 1 of the Constitution sets the attendance and vote needed to pass an amendment. It does not cover the earlier readings.
Article 8 of the National Assembly Organization Act sets a general quorum of one-third for the Assembly's business. It applies where Article 174, item 1 does not and no special rule exists.

Neither the Constitution nor the law says how readings are held for amendments or what attendance and votes each reading needs. The Assembly may therefore decide this itself, provided it does not conflict with the Constitution.

The Assembly's rules of procedure require two-thirds attendance and a three-fourths vote for the second and third readings. They state no attendance number for the first reading and only require that the proposal go to review after general discussion.

In past practice, the first reading was usually opened with one-third attendance, but sometimes with two-thirds. The first reading does not pass the amendment, so the choice is a matter of self-regulation and does not violate the Constitution.

who: The National Assembly as an institution

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule implementing the Agricultural Development Act is unconstitutional because it denies tax exemption when farmland is inherited by only one heir. The court decided the rule is not unconstitutional, because the exemption exists to encourage multiple heirs to agree on one person taking the land, so farmland is not split into small pieces.
raw.held: The implementing rule, which limits the exemption to cases where two or more co-heirs agree that one heir inherits or takes over the farmland, stays within the authority the law grants, is necessary for the public interest, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Agricultural Development Act aims to speed up agricultural development, and it pursues this by encouraging larger-scale farming and by banning the splitting of farmland or its transfer into co-ownership.

Article 31 exempts estate or gift tax when one able heir inherits or takes over family-farm land and keeps farming, and it comes with other benefits, such as land tax exemption and loan help. A former estate and gift tax provision likewise gave deductions for farmland, to support the farming policy.
These tax benefits are meant to encourage two or more co-heirs to agree, where possible, that one heir takes the land, so the land is not divided too finely and farming is not harmed.
When there is only one heir, there is no division or co-ownership through inheritance, so the exemption is not needed as an incentive and does not apply.

The implementing rule, Article 21, defines one-heir inheritance as co-heirs under the Civil Code agreeing that one takes over. This matches the law's purpose and meaning, does not exceed its authorization, and is necessary for the public interest.

who: Co-heirs who agree on one heir taking farmland

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Labor Union Act that bars staff of government administration and education enterprises from forming unions is constitutional as applied to technicians and workers in education. The court decided that banning education-sector technicians and manual workers (工友) from forming unions goes beyond what the Constitution allows and violates their freedom of association. The ban stops having effect within one year, and the legislature is to consider whether their labor rights need any limits.
raw.held: The part of Article 4 of the Labor Union Act that bars technicians and manual workers in education from organizing unions exceeds the necessary limit under Article 23 of the Constitution and infringes freedom of association. It loses effect from the date of the ruling, at the latest after one year, and the legislature should review within that time whether to limit how they exercise labor rights.

points.text: The Constitution protects freedom of association and calls for laws protecting workers; workers in all kinds of jobs may form unions to improve working conditions and their social and economic standing, which modern constitutional states widely recognize as a basic worker right.
Laws on unions should balance social order and the public interest while letting workers have rights such as collective bargaining and dispute rights.

These technicians and workers do only service work in education; although it relates to citizens' right to education, banning them from unions makes it hard for them to obtain reasonable rights and interests, going beyond the necessary limit in Article 23.

Unions can negotiate with employers on working conditions and welfare, conclude collective agreements, have disputes mediated, and strike by legal procedure after failed mediation, so a ban removes these means of protection.
Because their work is not wholly unconnected to campus safety and the teaching and research environment, the legislature should review within one year whether their labor rights need limits.

who: Technicians and manual workers in education

raw.answer: The case asked whether a lawyer disciplined by the Lawyers Disciplinary Review Committee can take that decision to administrative litigation. The court said no. It found the committees work like disciplinary courts attached to the High Court and the Supreme Court, so the review decision is a final court judgment, not an administrative act.
raw.held: The Lawyers Disciplinary Committee and Review Committee are in nature the first-instance and final disciplinary courts at the High Court and Supreme Court. The Review Committee's decision is a final court judgment, not an administrative disposition or appeal decision, so administrative litigation cannot be brought against it. Interpretation No. 295 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The constitutional right to sue means the right to seek relief from a court. A body set up within the judiciary, with judges and professionals, whose members act independently and whose procedures resemble court procedures, counts as equivalent to a court. Using such a body does not violate the right to sue.

Disciplinary bodies for most professions, such as accountants and architects, are committees set up by the competent authority and include professional group members, officials and experts. Lawyers are treated differently because their duties of protecting human rights and advancing justice are closely tied to the work of the courts.

The Lawyers Act sets the makeup of the two committees, with High Court judges and prosecutors, or Supreme Court judges and prosecutors, plus lawyers (and scholars on the review committee). Cases begin only when another agency or a bar association refers them.

The committees are organized within the High Court and Supreme Court, and their members are in substance as independent as those courts' judges. Their procedures on recusal, case assignment, evidence, records and deliberation follow the Code of Criminal Procedure or resemble court procedure.

Having lawyers or scholars on the committees is normal for professional discipline and does not change their character as disciplinary courts, unlike disciplinary bodies of other professions that belong to administrative agencies.

So the Review Committee's decision is a final court judgment, not an administrative act or appeal decision, and cannot be challenged in administrative litigation. The court also suggested renaming the committees as courts when the law is next amended.

who: Other professionals, such as accountants, with disciplinary bodies in administrative agencies

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Trademark Act's rule barring anyone from seeking to invalidate a registered trademark once it has been registered for ten years violates the constitutional protection of property. The court held that the ten-year limit does not conflict with Article 15 of the Constitution. It said the limit balances the public interest and private interests.
raw.held: The rule that a trademark registration similar to another person's registered trademark for the same or similar goods can no longer be challenged after ten years does not violate the Constitution's protection of property rights (Article 15).

points.text: Trademark rights are a form of property protected by Article 15, but the law may restrict them when needed for the public interest.
Letting interested parties seek invalidation of a confusingly similar trademark keeps market trade in order, protects the earlier trademark owner, and spares consumers from confusion.
Mistaken registrations are hard to avoid because they involve fact-finding on whether marks and goods are the same or similar, so a remedy is needed to protect earlier owners and consumers.
A mistakenly registered mark that has been used for years has built up goodwill that should also be protected.

Out of respect for the existing legal situation, after a considerable period the defect is treated as cured and no invalidation can be sought; the ruling takes this period to be ten years, based on related provisions of the Act.
Whether ten years is the right length is for the legislature to decide, and invalidating a mark as similar must still be done in good faith because registration creates reliance interests.

who: Owners of trademarks registered in error

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent is unconstitutional when it says a person can only ask the administrative court to suspend enforcement of an official decision after already filing an administrative lawsuit. The court held that the rule matches the Administrative Litigation Act and does not restrict people's right to sue, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
