raw.held: Asking the administrative court to suspend enforcement of the original decision requires that an administrative lawsuit has already been filed and is pending. The precedent saying so does not restrict the right to sue and is not unconstitutional.

points.text: Under Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act (formerly Article 11), enforcement is not stopped just because a lawsuit is filed, but the administrative court or the deciding agency may suspend it. So a request to the court requires a pending lawsuit.

Before a lawsuit is filed, a person who faces hard-to-repair harm in an urgent situation can ask the original agency or the appeals body to suspend enforcement under the proviso of Article 23 of the Petition Act.

If that agency refuses or does not respond in time, the person can object in the main dispute over the decision and may seek compensation for harm, so there is no need to ask the administrative court first.

The precedent, Administrative Court 1958 Ruling No. 26, is consistent with this, including that without the prior appeal step no lawsuit is allowed and so no suspension request to the court is allowed. It does not restrict the right to sue.

Whether a person who can show serious irreparable harm should be allowed to ask the court to set a temporary status before filing suit is left to be resolved by legislation when the administrative litigation system is reformed.

who: Agencies that issued or review decisions

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Audit Department Organization Act's rule that the Auditor General serves a six-year term is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not, because the term is meant to keep the post secure so the officeholder can act independently. The court also said the Auditor General is not a political appointee who leaves when the ruling party or policy changes.
raw.held: The six-year term for the Auditor General in Article 3 of the Audit Department Organization Act does not conflict with the Constitution. The Auditor General, appointed under Article 104 of the Constitution, is different from political officials who step down when the ruling party or policy changes.

points.text: The Auditor General holds an important post, overseeing audit work such as budget execution, payment orders, financial accounts and spotting unlawful or disloyal conduct in finances.
The main duty is auditing final accounts, which is closely tied to the legislature's review of budgets, so the Constitution gives the legislature a consent power over the appointment.

To protect independent auditing, laws give audit personnel protection: they exercise their powers independently without interference, and certain officers cannot be suspended, dismissed or transferred without a legal reason.
Other countries set the head auditor's post as lifetime or for a fixed term (for example 15, 12 or 7 years), so a fixed term is consistent with that practice.

The six-year term secures the officeholder's position so they can act independently without hesitation, which means the post differs from political appointees who leave with changes of party or policy.
Rules that group the Auditor General with political appointees on pay, retirement rewards and asset declarations are a matter of drafting convenience and do not change that status.

raw.answer: The case asked whether workers who stayed on after a state-run business was privatized could also get the extra six months' pay that the law gives to workers who left at the time of transfer. The court held that they cannot get it when their past years of service are settled at the time of transfer. They receive it only if they are laid off within five years after the transfer.
raw.held: Under Article 8 of the Statute for Transforming Public Enterprises into Private Enterprises, paragraph 2 covers workers who do not move over, and paragraph 3 covers workers kept on. Paragraph 2's standard applies to kept-on workers only for settling their past years of service, and at the time of transfer they do not receive the extra six months' pay.

points.text: Paragraph 2 covers workers who do not move over to the private business, and paragraph 3 covers workers who are kept on.

Paragraph 3 says only that past years of service are settled under paragraph 2's standard. It does not say the extra pay is settled that way too, so paragraph 2's standard applies only to the settlement of years of service.

The extra pay is not in the Labor Standards Act, so kept-on workers could not claim it under that Act. That is why the law did not need to say expressly that they get no six months' pay. Notice pay is different, so the law expressly excludes it.
Kept-on workers who are laid off within five years of transfer receive the extra six months' pay and notice pay then. This keeps their treatment in line with workers who left at transfer.

If kept-on workers also got the extra pay at transfer, they could be laid off the next day and collect it twice. That would encourage workers to stay and leave later, which the legislature did not intend.
The ruling is a unified interpretation of the existing law based on its wording and logic. It does not address what the legislature should do.

who: Workers who did not move over to the privatized business

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Code rule that a bigamous marriage is void is unconstitutional. The court said the rule is generally consistent with the Constitution. It found a problem in one special situation: a person marries in good faith relying on a final court judgment that ended the other person's earlier marriage, and that judgment is later changed. In that situation the later marriage should be kept valid.
raw.held: The rule voiding bigamous marriages is generally constitutional, but it fails to cover the special case of a good-faith marriage relying on a final judgment, and it should be reviewed and amended. Until then, it stops applying to such marriages. If both marriages end up existing at once, the other spouse of the bigamist may ask a court for divorce.

points.text: The voiding rule protects the social order of one-man-one-woman marriage, so in ordinary cases it does not conflict with the Constitution.
Unmarried adults of marriageable age have a freedom to marry, protected by Article 22 of the Constitution.
When a later marriage becomes bigamous only because a court's final judgment was later changed, it differs from ordinary bigamy because it results from conflicting court judgments.

The earlier judgment's hidden flaw may not have been known or knowable to the later spouse. A person who did not know and could not have known acted in good faith without fault, and under the principle of protecting reliance the later marriage should stay valid.
Good faith and lack of fault are factual questions for a court. Such a marriage is void only if a court judgment says so; otherwise it stays valid.

The rule does not address these special cases or matters like the legitimate status of children of the later marriage, and the existing provision on child custody is not enough, so it must be reviewed. Until then it is suspended for these marriages, and the other spouse may seek divorce if both marriages coexist.

who: People who married in good faith relying on a final judgment
Spouses of those in resulting double marriages
Women whose freedom to marry is protected

raw.answer: The case asked whether Interior Ministry rules on registering a superficies (land-use) right gained through long-term possession are unconstitutional. Those rules require the applicant to state the landowner's current and registered addresses, and the heir's details if the owner has died. The court held the rules themselves are constitutional, but they cannot be applied to block registration where it is objectively impossible to find the owner's or manager's name or address.
raw.held: The requirement to fill in the owner's details is consistent with the Constitution. However, where it is proven that the owner's or manager's name or address objectively cannot be found, so the right cannot be registered, the rule combination violates property protection and is not to be applied to that extent.

points.text: Acquiring property rights through long possession is meant to push original owners to use their property responsibly and to respect long-settled order, and rights acquired this way are constitutionally protected.

A superficies right is a limited right that sits on top of ownership, so requiring applicants to state the owner's details is necessary to protect the owner's interests and does not conflict with the Constitution.
If the details are not filled in, the land registration rules require the applicant to correct the omission, and the application is rejected if they do not.

The Ministry's requirements supplement those rules, and applied together they can make registration impossible when the owner's or manager's name or address objectively cannot be found, which conflicts with the constitutional protection of property.
To that extent, the rules should not be applied.

who: Possessors applying to register a superficies right by long possession
Managers of ancestral trusts, temples or deity associations that own land

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Civil Code rule giving the father the final say when parents disagree about exercising rights over their minor children is unconstitutional. The court found that this part of Article 1089 conflicts with the constitutional guarantees of equality between men and women and the elimination of sex discrimination. It ordered the rule reviewed and amended, and it loses effect within two years at the latest.
raw.held: The part of Civil Code Article 1089 that lets the father decide when parents disagree about exercising rights over minor children is inconsistent with the Constitution's equality provisions. It must be reviewed and revised, and it will lose effect no later than two years after the ruling is published.

points.text: The Constitution (Article 7 and Article 9, paragraph 5 of the Additional Articles) guarantees equality regardless of sex and calls for eliminating sex discrimination, and these apply to marriage and family life.
Differences in treatment based on sex are allowed only in special exceptional cases, based on physical differences between men and women or on differences in social roles that result from them.
The rule dates from 1930 and reflected tradition and the social conditions of that time, but education and job opportunities for women have since become nearly equal to men's.

If parents cannot agree, the rule gives the father the last word without considering the mother's position. This conflicts with gender equality and does not match women's actual standing in family life.

The court said a replacement should follow gender equality and the child's best interests, for example by letting the nearest elder relatives, a family council or a family court decide, with different arrangements considered for urgent situations.

who: Legislators who must revise the law

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent that stopped students from challenging school disciplinary decisions was unconstitutional. The court decided that when a school expels a student or imposes a similar penalty, that is an administrative disposition the student can challenge, after using the school's internal complaint process. The old precedent is no longer to be applied to the extent it conflicts with this.
raw.held: Expulsion or similar penalties that change a student's status and cost them educational opportunities are administrative dispositions. Students who exhaust the school's internal complaint process without relief may file an administrative appeal and a lawsuit, and the conflicting part of Administrative Court precedent No. 6 (1952 ruling, 41 Pan) is not to be applied.

points.text: The Constitution protects the right to education, and a person whose constitutional rights are unlawfully harmed may seek a final remedy from the courts regardless of their status, as earlier interpretations have explained.

Public schools are government bodies, and private schools are authorized by law to exercise public power in admitting, registering, disciplining and graduating students, so both have a status comparable to an agency when handling these matters.
Expulsion or similar penalties change student status and harm educational opportunities, so they are administrative dispositions that seriously affect the constitutional right to education.

Whether a penalty can be challenged depends on its content: minor ones needed to keep order and meeting educational goals, such as demerits or reprimands, go only through internal complaints, while expulsion or similar penalties may be challenged after the internal process.

The old precedent said students could only ask a supervising authority for correction, not file an administrative appeal. To the extent it conflicts with this ruling, it is not applied, to protect the rights to education and to sue.

Bodies and courts hearing such cases should respect the professional decisions of teachers and schools on conduct, academic evaluation and choice of discipline, and may only revoke or change them if unlawful or clearly improper.

who: Students facing expulsion or similar penalties
